blocks.x: In the second episode of Gilmore Girls Season 7, Lorelai deals with the aftermath of sleeping with Christopher (David Sutcliffe), Rory’s biological father, which angers her daughter. Rory is also upset about her long-planned Asia trip with Logan getting canceled, and Lorelai tries to cheer her up by creating an Asia-themed “wonderland” at home. Meanwhile, Rory’s best friend, Lane (Keiko Agena), returns from a disastrous honeymoon with shocking news.

The seventh and final season of Gilmore Girls is widely considered one of the most controversial seasons, with its character arcs, plotlines, and tropes dividing fans in their opinions. And the very second episode, "That's What You Get, Folks, For Makin' Whoopee,” proves that. One of the worst elements of this episode is Lorelai’s feeble attempt to bring an Asian experience to Rory, with a cartoonish, inappropriate aesthetic, which depicts cultural stereotyping and insensitivity to outdated tropes. 'Gilmore Girls: A Year in the Life', Episode 3

blocks.c: Lauren Graham and Alexis Bledel as Lorelai and Rory Gilmore, sitting poolside and laughing in the Summer episode of Gilmore Girls: A Year in the Life

blocks.x: In the third episode of the Gilmore Girls revival series, A Year in the Life, Rory takes up an unpaid editor job at the town’s local newspaper, the Star Hollow Gazette, in an attempt to keep it from shutting down. She is also offered an opportunity to write a book about her and Lorelai, which Lorelai instantly shuts down, leading to a huge mother-daughter fight. With the added chaos of the town’s bizarre musical, Lorelai decides to go on a journey of self-discovery.

When A Year in the Life was released, it certainly brought back the nostalgia that the show had come to be known for, but the four-episode revival also features the most uncomfortable element of the entire show. In the opening scene of the third episode, "Summer," Lorelai and Rory sit fully clothed by a public pool and make fun of other people wearing swimsuits, body-shaming everyday people and making harsh jokes. To some viewers at least, this kind of commentary appears to be in poor taste and mean-spirited, and fails to hold up in the context of modern perceptions of TV tropes.

blocks.c: To Live and Let Diorama Season 5 Episode 18

blocks.x: In this Season 5 episode of Gilmore Girls, an old resident of the town dies and leaves his house to the town to be run as a museum for the first two months, and Luke volunteers to help. Meanwhile, Rory, Paris, and Lane deal with relationship troubles while getting drunk on the punch at the Founder’s Day celebration. On the other side of the episode, Lorelai makes some unfiltered comments in a magazine interview.

Another episode of Gilmore Girls that has not aged well, “To Live and Let Diorama,” is not problematic today because of any offensive commentary or interpretations. Rather, the relationship dynamics and character tropes explored in the episode feel completely out of touch with today’s reality and have not aged well. Additionally, the museum gags don’t quite communicate small-town charm the way they used to and have been criticized for being fairly cringey now.

blocks.c: Rory (Alexis Bledel) dressed as Donna Reed in in the Gilmore Girls episode "That Damn Donna Reed"

blocks.x: This episode from the very first season of the show explores Rory and Dean’s budding romance as they begin their relationship and have their first fight. When Lorelai invites him to participate in the mother-daughter ritual of making fun of the titular hit television show from the '50s, Dean reveals that he supports traditional gender roles. Rory fights with Dean about his patriarchal views, but ends the evening by dressing up like Donna Reed and cooking him dinner.

"That Damn Donna Reed" has been criticized for its mixed signals on feminism and foreshadowing Dean’s toxic control. It mocks conventions of ‘50s lifestyles, while also romanticizing the same for its characters and ultimately reinforces the gender norms it initially set out to criticize. The episode also lays the early groundwork for Dean’s controlling behavior, which is explored later in the show, and to modern audiences, it all comes across as somewhat toxic.

And the very second episode, "That's What You Get, Folks, For Makin' Whoopee,” proves that. One of the worst elements of this episode is Lorelai’s feeble attempt to bring an Asian experience to Rory, with a cartoonish, inappropriate aesthetic, which depicts cultural stereotyping and insensitivity to outdated tropes. The episode is also criticized for writing off Lane’s arc with a sudden pregnancy instead of giving her character positive closure.

5
“Summer”

'Gilmore Girls: A Year in the Life', Episode 3

Image via Netflix

In the third episode of the Gilmore Girls revival series, A Year in the Life, Rory takes up an unpaid editor job at the town’s local newspaper, the Star Hollow Gazette, in an attempt to keep it from shutting down. She is also offered an opportunity to write a book about her and Lorelai, which Lorelai instantly shuts down, leading to a huge mother-daughter fight. With the added chaos of the town’s bizarre musical, Lorelai decides to go on a journey of self-discovery.

When A Year in the Life was released, it certainly brought back the nostalgia that the show had come to be known for, but the four-episode revival also features the most uncomfortable element of the entire show. In the opening scene of the third episode, "Summer," Lorelai and Rory sit fully clothed by a public pool and make fun of other people wearing swimsuits, body-shaming everyday people and making harsh jokes. To some viewers at least, this kind of commentary appears to be in poor taste and mean-spirited, and fails to hold up in the context of modern perceptions of TV tropes.

6
“To Live and Let Diorama”

Season 5, Episode 18

Image via WB

In this Season 5 episode of Gilmore Girls, an old resident of the town dies and leaves his house to the town to be run as a museum for the first two months, and Luke volunteers to help. Meanwhile, Rory, Paris, and Lane deal with relationship troubles while getting drunk on the punch at the Founder’s Day celebration. On the other side of the episode, Lorelai makes some unfiltered comments in a magazine interview.

Another episode of Gilmore Girls that has not aged well, “To Live and Let Diorama,” is not problematic today because of any offensive commentary or interpretations. Rather, the relationship dynamics and character tropes explored in the episode feel completely out of touch with today’s reality and have not aged well. Additionally, the museum gags don’t quite communicate small-town charm the way they used to and have been criticized for being fairly cringey now.

7
“That Damn Donna Reed”

Season 1, Episode 14

Image via The WB

This episode from the very first season of the show explores Rory and Dean’s budding romance as they begin their relationship and have their first fight. When Lorelai invites him to participate in the mother-daughter ritual of making fun of the titular hit television show from the '50s, Dean reveals that he supports traditional gender roles. Rory fights with Dean about his patriarchal views, but ends the evening by dressing up like Donna Reed and cooking him dinner.

"That Damn Donna Reed" has been criticized for its mixed signals on feminism and foreshadowing Dean’s toxic control. It mocks conventions of ‘50s lifestyles, while also romanticizing the same for its characters and ultimately reinforces the gender norms it initially set out to criticize. The episode also lays the early groundwork for Dean’s controlling behavior, which is explored later in the show, and to modern audiences, it all comes across as somewhat toxic.
